summary: Describes the use of HDLC-like framing for PPP encapsulated packets. It is an Internet Standard.

eli5.summary: On a serial line, messages need clear start and end markers. This describes how PPP marks them.

questions: what is the ppp flag sequence 0x7e
how does ppp escape control characters
what is the ppp async control character map
subtitle: How PPP wraps its packets in HDLC-style frames so they can travel over serial and other point-to-point links.

tldr.problem: PPP sends packets over a stream of bits or bytes, so the receiver needs to know where each packet starts and ends, how to carry any byte value safely, and how to detect damage.
tldr.mechanism: Each packet is placed between 0x7e Flag Sequences with fixed Address (0xff) and Control (0x03) fields and a 16-bit or 32-bit Frame Check Sequence. Byte-oriented links escape special octets with 0x7d, and bit-oriented links insert a 0 bit after five 1 bits.
tldr.outcome: It is an Internet Standard (STD 51) that obsoletes RFC 1549 and defines the Async-Control-Character-Map option for negotiating which control characters must be escaped.

today: RFC 1662 is an Internet Standard (STD 51) and, per the unit metadata, has not been obsoleted or updated. It obsoletes RFC 1549.

sections.title: Scope and Physical Layer Needs
sections.content:
RFC 1662 describes HDLC-like framing for packets carried by the Point-to-Point Protocol (RFC 1661). It covers bit-oriented and octet-oriented synchronous links, and asynchronous links with 8 bits of data and no parity. The links MUST be full-duplex, and may be dedicated or circuit-switched.

An escape mechanism lets control data such as XON/XOFF pass through transparently and removes spurious control data that intervening equipment may inject. PPP detects errors with the HDLC Frame Check Sequence, which is common in hardware and which the RFC also supplies in software.

The only absolute physical requirement is a full-duplex circuit that is transparent to PPP frames. PPP presents an octet interface, imposes no transmission rate limit and does not require control signals such as RTS, CTS, DCD or DTR. When such signals exist they SHOULD be used to signal the Up and Down events to LCP. Without them, the implementation MUST signal Up on initialization and SHOULD NOT signal Down.
sections.eli5: This describes the kind of wire PPP needs: one where both sides can talk at the same time. PPP does not care how fast it is.

sections.title: The HDLC-like Frame
sections.content:
A standard frame is sent left to right as: Flag, Address, Control, Protocol, Information, Padding, FCS, Flag. The Protocol, Information and Padding fields come from the PPP encapsulation in RFC 1661.

  • Flag Sequence: 01111110 (0x7e) begins and ends every frame. One flag is enough between two frames, and two consecutive flags form an empty frame that is silently discarded and not counted as an FCS error.
  • Address: one octet, 0xff, the All-Stations address. It MUST always be recognized and received. Frames with unrecognized Addresses SHOULD be silently discarded.
  • Control: one octet, 0x03, the Unnumbered Information command with the Poll/Final bit set to zero.
  • FCS: 16 bits by default, sent least significant octet first. A 32-bit FCS may be negotiated through RFC 1570. It covers the Address, Control, Protocol, Information and Padding fields, not the flags, the FCS itself, or any start and stop bits or octets added for transparency.

LCP can negotiate changes to this frame. With Address-and-Control-Field-Compression, the two fields are simply omitted on transmission. A receiver checks whether the first two octets are 0xff and 0x03; if not, it assumes they were compressed away. The Protocol value 0x00ff is reserved to avoid ambiguity when Protocol-Field-Compression is on.
sections.eli5: Each message is like a letter in a standard envelope with the same stamp mark at the front and back. A short check number at the end lets the receiver see if the letter got scrambled.

sections.title: Octet-stuffed Framing
sections.content:
On asynchronous and octet-synchronous links, the transmitter uses octet stuffing. The Control Escape octet is 0x7d. After computing the FCS, the sender replaces each Flag Sequence, each Control Escape octet, and each octet flagged in its sending Async-Control-Character-Map with 0x7d followed by the original octet XORed with 0x20. At a minimum, senders MUST escape the flag and the Control Escape octet, and receivers MUST process all escape sequences.

On reception, before the FCS is computed, any octet below 0x20 that is flagged in the receive map is removed, since equipment on the path may have inserted it. Each Control Escape is removed and the next octet is XORed with 0x20, unless that next octet is a flag, which aborts the frame.

Frames are silently discarded, without counting an FCS error, if they are too short (under 4 octets with the 16-bit FCS), end with a Control Escape followed by a closing flag, or violate octet framing.

Time fill differs by link type. Octet-synchronous links have no inter-octet fill and MUST send flags between frames. Asynchronous links MUST fill with continuous 1 bits, and a single flag may close one frame and open the next. Because noise can corrupt the next frame in that case, transmitters SHOULD send an opening flag when appreciable time has passed since the last closing flag, which is likely no more than about 1 second. Asynchronous octets are sent least significant bit first, with one start bit, eight data bits and one stop bit.
sections.eli5: If a secret code word shows up inside the message, the sender puts a warning sign in front of it and disguises it a bit. The receiver spots the sign and undoes the disguise.

sections.title: Bit-stuffed Framing
sections.content:
On bit-synchronous links the receiver watches the bit stream for the flag pattern 01111110. To stop data from imitating a flag, the transmitter inserts a 0 bit after every run of five contiguous 1 bits, including the last five bits of the FCS. The receiver discards any 0 that directly follows five 1 bits, before computing the FCS.

The "shared zero mode" flag 011111101111110 SHOULD NOT be used because it hinders interoperability with converters. Frames are silently discarded if they are under 4 octets with the 16-bit FCS or end with more than six 1 bits. Flags SHOULD fill the gaps between frames. If a circuit-switched link needs mark idle, the sender MUST keep at least 15 consecutive 1 bits between flags, which differs from ISO 3309's 7 to 14 bits.

For line encoding, the RFC says NRZ is most widely available at 56 Kbps through 2.0 Mbps and recommends it as the default, with NRZI as an alternative. NRZI makes the 16-bit FCS miss one error in 215 and miss triple errors, so the RFC recommends negotiating the 32-bit FCS when NRZI is used.
sections.eli5: Here the sender sneaks in an extra zero whenever five ones in a row show up, so the data can never look like the start marker.

sections.title: Negotiating the Control Character Map
sections.content:
The Async-Control-Character-Map (ACCM) is an LCP option, type 2, length 6, that tells the peer which control characters must remain escaped on an asynchronous link. Each end keeps two maps: a 32-bit receiving map, and a sending map of up to 256 bits.

The ACCM field is four octets, sent most significant octet first. Each bit matches the octet of the same value: a bit set to one means that octet MUST stay mapped, and a bit cleared to zero means it need not be. The default for asynchronous links is 0xffffffff, which covers all ASCII control characters except DEL. For other link types the default is 0.

The RFC notes that it is rarely necessary to map all control characters. The peer SHOULD Configure-Nak with the logical union of the sets of mapped octets. A transmitter may also escape octets from 0x40 to 0xff (except 0x5e), but that does not solve problems for receivers that cannot handle all non-control characters or for 7-bit links.

Asynchronous-to-synchronous converters do all stuffing conversion themselves. For that reason a synchronous PPP implementation MUST always answer the ACCM option with Configure-Ack, without doing any mapping itself.
sections.eli5: The two sides agree on a list of letters that are dangerous on this wire. Only those letters get the special disguise, so nothing extra is done for safe ones.

sections.title: Recommended Options and the FCS Code
sections.content:
Appendix A recommends Magic Number, Link Quality Monitoring and no address, control or protocol field compression for high speed links. For low speed or asynchronous links it recommends the ACCM, Magic Number and both compressions.

Appendix B shows octet sequences that begin a valid PPP LCP frame, such as 7e ff 03 c0 21, so a login process can notice that the peer has started speaking PPP. Appendix C gives a table generator and C code for computing the FCS. The 16-bit version uses the generator polynomial x0 + x5 + x12 + x16, starts from 0xffff and yields the good final value 0xf0b8. The 32-bit version starts from 0xffffffff and yields 0xdebb20e3.

A receiver can keep calculating over the incoming bytes until the closing flag and then check for the good FCS value, which is how the FCS suits hardware.
sections.eli5: The back of the memo has a ready-made recipe for the check number, so everyone calculates it the same way.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The link layer might not be told when the connected state of the physical layer changes. That can cause security lapses from over-reliance on the integrity and security of switching systems and administrations. An insertion attack might go undetected, and an attacker who can spoof the same calling identity might avoid link authentication.

The same concern appears in the physical layer section, which advises signalling the Down event whenever significant time has elapsed since a link was disconnected, because the price of faster setup is decreased security.
sections.eli5: If nobody tells the link when the phone line was swapped, a sneaky person could slip in. So the link should be told when connections change.
